newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich asks Republicans to end internal strife.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich asks Republicans to end internal strife.

text.p: Newt Gingrich, speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives and still in charge of fractious Republicans, asked his colleagues on Wednesday to put to rest the "tiresome and overwrought saga" of plots against him and get back to work.

Telling his colleagues, "I'm speaker and I'm in charge," the Georgia Republican agreed to requests for a "family discussion" on Wednesday night and told them that once it was held there would be no more talk of the party struggles.

"I strongly encourage every Republican member to participate in this dialogue. Let me emphasise: I will not allow another chapter to be written in this tiresome and overwrought saga. This discussion will be the end of the story," Gingrich said as divided and anxious Republicans began a routine morning meeting to discuss upcoming legislation.

Representative Sherwood Boehlert of New York, a Gingrich supporter, echoed many in saying he felt the party's mainstream would rally around him. "If I didn't know better I would think this was a Machiavellian plot devised by the speaker because he emerges 10 feet tall."

While no decisions and no votes of confidence in the leadership are expected, lawmakers said three of the speaker's top deputies must give explanations of their recent actions and will face questions on their role in the aborted coup.
"It's not an inquisition, not a vote of confidence. It is a discussion," Representative Robert Ney of Ohio said.

A group of conservative dissidents said they were given reason to believe their aborted effort to oust the speaker earlier this month would have support from some in the leadership. Several of them mentioned a role played by Republican Whip Tom DeLay of Texas, who has not addressed their concerns as yet but has said he will not resign.

In addition to DeLay, sitting on the hot seats will be Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas, who has vehemently denied involvement and professed his allegiance to Gingrich, and Republican Conference chairman John Boehner of Ohio, who has said he was unaware of the plot.
But several lawmakers doubted the strife can be ended so easily.

"I think it is going to be pretty hard for the bad feelings to go away. These are pretty deep-seated feelings," Representative Ray LaHood of Illinois said. "I hope people come away with a better understanding of what these three leaders were up to," he added.

Republican unrest grew this year as the party returned from the 1996 elections with a narrowed majority in the House and less political leverage to use in talks with President Bill Clinton on crucial budget and tax issues.
This has proved particularly disturbing to a group of conservatives, many of whom were swept to power in 1994 when the party reclaimed its majority after 40 years.
